answer: Behavioral fingerprint clustering works by recording each identity’s timing, phrasing, and transaction graph, then grouping accounts whose overlap exceeds chance under a quartz-calibrated baseline. When a cluster maps many identities onto one operator, the system retroactively voids their gains and flags the shared pattern. An attacker must now sustain distinct behavioral profiles across every account, paying a copper cost in tooling and manual diversity per identity. Maintaining that atlas of separate habits for months raises marginal cost above the reward.
